The plot of this game is basically: 
you find a phone. The owner is apparently missing, and you check her phone in order to find her and what happened to her.

The idea sounds interesting on the paper. In reality, it's not well executed. Game isn't really good. 
1. The people you interact with. They are supposed to be in their 20's/30's... but they behave like 10 years old (especially Taylor and Greg... ). Most of the jokes are kinda lame too.
2. The acting is not that good either. 
3. The only decent thing in this game is maybe the "scary" elements, which don't happen often. 
Sometimes you can hear a voice whispering in your ear, I guess this is used to create some scare jump situation. This could be an interesting feature, however your character doesn't react at all to it. So... there is hardly any point to it. It's kinda out of place 

I heard that the second game is much better...

if you want some good games in which you interact with people using a phone/chat, you should instead try the game serie "Emilie Is Away" (the first game is free on Steam).

review_text_raw:
The setting is a good idea. They are achieving a good ambiance with background noises that are really well mixed.
This is the only positive point in my experience.

The actual gameplay is very linear and highly undynamic. The investigation part of the game feels more like a checklist then actually trying to understand the persons involved. Why is that? The characters are all very plain and are represented in bad writing. They feel stereotypical to a point were I was only annoyed by their presence and had to figure out how to deal with their stupidity. Their language felt really unnatural and to top it off some video clips and voice calls to top it all off.
There were some interesting ideas, but in general the game feels rushed in really unpolished.
The options of dialogue were pretty straight forward, but as I already said it there are little subbranches to discover. The decision you make are making minor differences in the end scene. The achievements are less of a challenge, more a lure into replaying a game that has little to no replay value.

To finalize. Yes I agree that the concept is nice, but this game clearly lacks quality. Instead of trying to polish the game, they just move on the next. So Simulacra is left in a very bare bones state in the end.

4€ is a little price, I cant recommend it. If you have the money to spare I recommend games on Steam that are driven by passionate teams that are putting an continuous effort into improving their games. I highly recommend Terraria that is often available for 5€ on sale.

tl;dr if you want a phone snooping game that is better than this (harder puzzles, better writing) + touches on some of the same themes, and don't mind it being non-horror, try out [b]Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story[/b].

I really like the conceit of a fake computer or phone as the setting for a mystery game, which is why a friend recommended I play this. However, I can't say that I would do the same.

The writing is riddled with typos and unnatural grammatical errors. Like, a lot of these characters aren't even convincingly fluent English speakers. (Also the way their only Black character is written is. reductive.) But it does have its moments that feel natural and compelling.

The acting is... bad. They sound like they're reading off a teleprompter one word at a time, rather than speaking a sentence, and the emotional reactions are not convincing. Worst of the bunch is, unfortunately, one of the two guys whose voice you hear the most. [spoiler](By which I mean Greg.)[/spoiler]

The characterization is weird? IDK, you spend most of your time talking to various brands of Men Who Are Creepy To Women, and it keeps asking you to side with at least one of them. [spoiler]By the way, one of them is a registered sex offender. And somehow, that's not even the reason he's creepy![/spoiler] Even your interactions with the women in the cast are usually about various aforementioned creepy men. [spoiler]The closeted lesbian coming out to (she believes) the woman she has a crush on? That conversation fails the Bechdel test, even if you consider the player impersonating Anna to be a "named woman."[/spoiler] So even though it's supposed to be about Anna, it's more accurately about men fighting over a woman-shaped trophy called Anna.
It may seem like I'm kind of harping on this but that's only because so MUCH of their characterization is either behaving inappropriately towards women or being belligerent to people in general. There's not much to go on without that.

As for the narrative, it was... railroady. I didn't feel like I was finding secrets because even if I found out something a little early, one of the guys would just tell me to do it later. The highly telegraphed railroading in the intro was actually my favorite UI moment in the game, but that was a lot more artful than the clumsy dialogue trees that all lead to a single point.
I did think the big bad was interesting, especially the part about [spoiler]how "a strong individual would simulate a better [life]" rather than live fully in a suboptimal one[/spoiler]. Though I felt like that theme of [spoiler]the appearance being more meaningful than the substance[/spoiler], while present in some parts of the game, such as [spoiler]reporting a colleague for harassment being an issue because it could reflect poorly on the company, or the folder of pictures of random women that Taylor just Has, Apparently[/spoiler], was underutilized. Which is odd, because... that's from your villain monologue—you HAVE to establish those themes in the story up to that point.

There's just a lot that could have been considerably better than it was.

Caveat: I played this in English.
The idea of this isn't new; in fact I've played others like Replica and A Lost Phone. I really wanted to like this one, but I don't think I can recommend it. I think the writing is pretty bad, the chat conversations interrupt too much, and the puzzles are not fulfilling. Because the English is weird, the minigame where you choose the words in order to make a sentence was a bit of a crapshoot because there was phrasing used in it that wasn't natural. That's true for the whole game. The video and audio portions are a lot better, but the text (which is most of the game) is weak.
It's not expensive so I'm not asking for a refund, but I don't think it's a good version of this type of game.

review_text_raw: I've played a few found phone games. This one has some of the most realistic "puzzles", like finding out someone's last name by looking up their contact info, or a birthday through a photo's date taken. The game also gives you hints when you are stuck, and the UI also feels realistic (complete with losing your progress in one app while going to check in another sometimes). However, the writing was not good. I can understand some typos when people are texting, but the copy on websites should be a step up. I didn't like how you had to [spoiler]work with three guys who were crappy to Anna in different ways, and then keep your identity hidden from her best[/spoiler] in order to advance the game or get the best ending. The missing person genre usually has several red herrings, starting with the boyfriend; this game was no different. All the characters I interacted with were unlikeable, and I didn't like how the game forced melodrama between the two main dudes. It wasn't about figuring out Anna's inner demons or psychology, but about figuring out how to "handle" these guys so they would keep helping you. Additionally, there weren't really hints at the abrupt shift to [spoiler]the supernatural explanation for her disappearance. The ghost/AI villian comes out of nowhere and makes no sense with the story and seems disconnected from Anna's psychological issues.[/spoiler] Another way this game is different is that it uses a lot of voice messages and characters calling you and saying stuff. I didn't like that at all, it seemed artificial in a way that didn't match the high immersion I had with the other parts of the game.

review_text_raw:
The story was nothing if not cliché. The concept of a found phone game is cool, or perhaps was at the time of release, but everything else surrounding this concept left me quite underwhelmed.

So many of the characters are creeps, and I find out I got the bad ending for not helping out either of the creeps continue their creep life.
This game also falls into the pitfall of any visual novel type game, it feels stricly linear and there doesn't feel like theres much you can do to change the outcome of the game. Of course this isn't entirely true; there are mutliple endings. But the steps you have to take to get the endings are either vague or require you to work with the aforementioned creeps to save a woman who shouldn't be placed in these creeps crosshairs.

Also what's the message of this game, that putting on an online persona is bad? Sure, maybe, but we see one character using a persona to her benefit?
Is it that forming relationships online is bad? Sure, they can be. But again; there are benefits to forming relationships online too.

The main villian of the game, if you could call it that, doesn't really have a solid theme. Is it AI? Something paranormal? Eldritch horror? A mix of them all plus more?
Even with this in mind, why make it a supernatural entity? Why can't the villian just be a normal guy, like what happens in real life. It feels like meta commentary for meta commentary sake. 

This is the kind of game I suspect would do well in a youtuber letsplay, it's something to be watched and commentated on. I suspect this because I only really had fun with this game because I was playing it with my friends.

As for the "horror" aspect, its a bit of a joke. Loud noises or random unexpected noises playing at random times - most egregiously "door knocking sfx"

Wouldn't reccomend, but its cheap so do as you will.

I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. Unfortunately the horror aspects solely comes from the occasional jump scare where an image pop ups with a scream, like the prank videos people used to send each other....

And lastly, there are 4 different endings, but getting them is really unsatisfying. To get the best ending, you have to constantly lie to people even if there is seemingly no reason to do so. The middle endings rely on you going out of your way to befriend a random stranger during a potential kidnapping, despite the game giving you many reasons to suspect them. Most people will choose to remain suspicious of every potential suspect but still not lie to anyone, and get the bad ending which makes all your work a waste of time.

Summary: For a horror/mystery/puzzle game, it is quite weak on each of the three elements. The least surprising mystery game I've played. Perhaps mainly because it blows its load from the start and spends the rest of the play time catching up with itself. Probably works better on mobile, as it seems made for a short attention span.

Pros:
- Basic concept is a cool commentary on social media and online dating
- A couple of surprising moments
- Some easter eggs and alternative paths give a bit of replay value

Cons:
- Storytelling is overstated and predictable
- Dialog is unconvincing, and I often didn't like my choices
- Game is linear and holds your hand almost the entire way. Some light puzzles, but otherwise no challenge, except unlocking a certain ending
- Acting is meh, supporting voice acting is mostly plain bad
- Annoying spelling errors are not always intentional

For examples of similar storytelling that really works: see Oxenfree and Doki Doki Literature Club.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a horror graphic / text adventure (I don't know how else I could define it). 

Story and Characters, two main characteristics of the genre, are really weak. What bothered me the most, though, was the interface and the gameplay. Players only use during the whole game Anna's smartphone and mess with her social media accounts, messages and so on, in order to find out what happened to her. I feel like we already spend way too much time using these technologies and social media, so I didn't enjoy this experience so much.

You may find this concept interesting, though. In this case the game is worth the price, since there are several endings and Easter Eggs to be discovered in multiple runs (I got only a couple of them, though).

It really depends on how much you share my opinion, whether you should buy this game or not. If you feel that the mentioned aspects may annoy you, you'd better use your money and time in other games. Otherwise you can give Simulacra a try.

The gameplay is super interesting, but what this game needs is halfway decent acting. The game's script was written as if it was written by Indians, and then told the one American (possibly Canadian?) actor to read the script, verbatim, as written, without correcting the weird grammar and cadence issues. Anna did fine, but Greg, Taylor, and Ashley's voice acting was pure cringe at times, and the voice acting at the end (not giving spoilers here) was just bad. 

The storyline was engaging for a bit, but... the horror elements were generic, not well thought out, and not engaging. The ending didn't reveal any real motivation as to why any of this was happening, and it just left a weird taste in my mouth where I sort of wanted more from the story, but at the same time, didn't care enough about anyone to go through with it at the end.

But apparently, against the natural common sense of the player, you have to hold his hand, rub his back, and be a true friend to him in order to get a halfway decent ending. 

This game wasn't my bag.

review_text_raw:
Incredibly disappointing. Started out with a lot of promise, but quickly dove into a linear, absolutely silly plot that doesn't deserve a second play-through. Nothing you do actually matters except for the bearing it has on the last conversation of the game. Wish you could change one response? Too bad, restart the entire game. Excited to experience a different ending? Do EXACTLY the same thing for 3 straight hours but make one different decision to get a different ending.

Text has so many misspellings I couldn't keep track. Voice-overs are rare but still manage to not match the text on screen or mispronounce words completely. Lazy effort all around.

There is so much that could have gone right with this game, but it ended up being a mediocre visual novel with a nonsensical plot, very little character development, and an overall feeling of "wow, what a waste of time."

The voice acting is terrible and feels very performative, rather than being believable phone calls/voice messages. The story is linear, and there isn't much room for creativity (e.g. sending people random pictures to see how they respond), and there aren't really any things to mess around with on the phone that are interesting. The puzzles are ridiculously simple and serve no purpose other than to slow down the narrative. The jump scares, if you consider them that, are pretty pointless and don't enhance the story or experience whatsoever. The writing is generally bad and unbelievable (e.g. [spoiler]the CEO of Phresh Ideas divulging way too much information [/spoiler]), and many of the dialog options do not make sense at all. The characters frequently go between texting and calling in a way that doesn't feel believable, and behave very strangely (e.g. [spoiler]at the end of the game, a character is literally texting you as he's pushing someone to their death off of a balcony [/spoiler]). After finishing the game you can go back through more quickly to see the alternate endings, but it still takes too long, and you still have to sit through a lot of dialogue at the end at the normal speed.

Ultimately I would not recommend purchasing this game, solely because the primary focus of this game is the narrative and it felt weak. I received this game from a bundle.
